front_blocks.md: Describe the pathway taken by water through a plant.

back_blocks.md: Absorbed from the soil by root hair cells (by osmosis).
Moves across the root to the xylem.
Transported up the stem in the xylem.
Moves into the leaf, evaporates from the cells and leaves through the stomata (transpiration).

The evaporation of water cools the leaves.

front_blocks.md: What apparatus is used to investigate the rate of transpiration, and what does it measure?

back_blocks.md: A potometer.
It measures the rate of water uptake by a shoot, which is used as a measure of the transpiration rate.

front_blocks.md: Outline how to use a potometer to investigate transpiration.

back_blocks.md: Cut a leafy shoot under water and fit it into the potometer.
Record the starting position of the air bubble.
Measure how far the bubble moves in a set time.
Repeat under different conditions (e.g. higher temperature or wind speed).

front_blocks.md: Explain why increasing temperature increases the rate of transpiration (Extended).

back_blocks.md: Higher temperature gives water molecules more energy.
They evaporate and diffuse out of the leaf faster, so transpiration increases.

front_blocks.md: Explain why increasing wind speed increases the rate of transpiration (Extended).

back_blocks.md: Wind blows away the water vapour around the leaf.
This maintains a steep concentration gradient, so water diffuses out faster.

front_blocks.md: Explain why high humidity decreases the rate of transpiration (Extended).

back_blocks.md: High humidity means there is already a lot of water vapour in the air.
This reduces the concentration gradient between the leaf and the air, so less water diffuses out.

back_blocks.md: The cells lose water faster than it is replaced, so they become flaccid.

front_blocks.md: How can wilting actually help reduce water loss?

back_blocks.md: Wilting reduces the surface area of the leaves exposed to the sun, which lowers the rate of transpiration.

front_blocks.md: What is meant by a 'source' and a 'sink' in translocation (Extended)?

back_blocks.md: Source: a part of the plant that makes or releases sucrose (e.g. the leaves).
Sink: a part that uses or stores sucrose (e.g. roots, growing tips, storage organs).

front_blocks.md: How does the direction of transport in the phloem differ from the xylem?

back_blocks.md: Phloem can transport food in both directions (up or down the plant).
Xylem only transports water in one direction (upwards).
